lab.name: Geotechnical Earthquake and GeoHazards Lab
lab.intro: Geotechnical Earthquake and GeoHazards Lab (GEHL) studies geotechnical earthquake engineering and geohazards to evaluate and predict the impact of earthquakes on infrastructure and urban areas. Our goal is to contribute to the development of more resilient urban systems against natural disasters. We combine geotechnical centrifuge modeling, numerical simulation, analytical methods, probabilistic approaches, and earthquake case histories to evaluate what has happened, predict what could happen, and design urban systems that stay resilient through natural disasters.

core.title: A reliable, realistic, and interactive seismic risk map
paragraphs: GEHL's vision is a seismic risk map that is reliable, realistic, and interactive: one that engineers, planners, and the public can trust and use. Every project in the lab is a step toward it, and every project follows one chain: characterize the input motion, identify the soil-foundation-structure system, and predict its output. The same framework is being extended from earthquakes to other natural hazards.

Reaching that map takes methods at every scale, from the laboratory to the city. Laboratory and centrifuge tests expose the micro-mechanics of soil at the particle scale; centrifuge and numerical modeling capture the response of single and multiple structures as one system; and site characterization, from shear-wave velocity profiles to earthquake case histories, builds the liquefaction hazard and ground-motion models behind the map. Experimental, numerical, and analytical results are checked against recorded earthquakes from databases such as DesignSafe, KiK-net, and CESMD, and probabilistic methods carry the uncertainty through to the final risk estimate.

framework.s: Soil, foundation, and structure systems: centrifuge tests, element tests, numerical simulations, subsurface modeling, and site characterization
System's engineering demand parameters: settlement, rotation, pore pressure, cracking, and erosion, with their uncertainty

areas.title: Dynamic Soil-Foundation-Structure Interaction
paragraphs: Seismic design usually treats the structure and the ground separately. We measure how they move together, so that the interaction can be used in design rather than ignored. Dynamic centrifuge tests on shallow foundations, rocking foundations, and disconnected piled rafts give the data; analytical models that couple horizontal structural response with foundation rocking and swaying turn the data into predictions.

areas.title: Energy-Based Soil Liquefaction Assessment
paragraphs:
We use the energy dissipated in the soil, rather than cyclic stress alone, to estimate the buildup of excess pore pressure. This makes it possible to evaluate liquefaction without pore-water-pressure transducers, to read the timing of liquefaction directly from recorded ground motions through the spectral energy ratio, and to treat dissipated energy as an index of liquefiability.
Ongoing work builds a multi-scale framework for integrated cyclic loadings and a probabilistic liquefaction hazard assessment.

areas.eyebrow: Research area 3 | Source, Path, and Site Effects
areas.title: Seismic Site Response Analysis, Ground Motion Modeling, and Topographic Effects
paragraphs: The motion that reaches a foundation depends on the source, the path, and the site. We work on seismic source and fault modeling, ground-motion characterization for Korean and global conditions, and one- and two-dimensional site response analysis, including the amplification caused by topography.

areas.title: Cracking and Concentrated Leak Erosion due to Fault Rupture
paragraphs: Many embankment dams sit on or near active faults. A vertical offset in the foundation can crack the crest, and water flowing through that crack can erode the core. We estimate crack dimensions from the offset and judge the erosion potential from the erodibility and swelling of the core material.
topics: Scaling of flow through transverse cracks

Dynamic soil-structure interaction (SSI) and structure-soil-structure interaction (SSSI)

courses.title: Introduction to Geotechnical Engineering
courses.text: The purpose of the course is to introduce students to Geotechnical Engineering terminology and fundamentals of soil mechanics – this course will cover topics viz: phase relationships, soil classification, compaction, effective stress of soil, fluid flow in soil, consolidation and settlement, shear strengths of soil. Adding to regular classes, this course also incorporates laboratory classes to provide students with hands-on experiences in soil mechanics. This course provides students with a firm foundation for advancing to more theoretical and applied areas in geotechnical engineering, including foundation engineering, dam engineering, soil dynamics, and geotechnical earthquake engineering.
outline: Course Introduction, Phase Diagram
Phase Relationships, Grain Size Distribution
Index Properties – Plasticity, Soil Classification
Clay Minerals, Soil Fabric
Compaction of Soils
Field Compaction
Effective Stress
Mid-term
Hydrostatic Water in Soils, Fluid Flow in Soils – Heads, Permeability
Fluid Flow in Soils – Seepage
Fluid Flow in Soils – 2D Flow
Compressibility of Soils
Time Rate of Consolidation
Stress Distribution and Settlement in a Soil Mass
Shear Strength and Failure of Soils
Final Exam

courses.title: Advanced Soil Dynamics
courses.text: The purpose of the course is to introduce students to Soil Dynamics – this course will cover topics viz: dynamics of simple systems (Fundamentals of waves and vibrations, SDOFs), dynamic soil properties (G/Gmax and damping strain relationship), waves in infinite and bounded media, and one-dimensional site response analysis. This course provides students with a firm foundation and theoretical knowledge for geotechnical earthquake engineering.
outline: Course Introduction, Fourier Transform
Harmonic Waves and Complex Numbers, Signal Processing (How to Sample)
Signal Processing (How to Process), SDOF System (Free Vibration)
SDOF System (Forced Vibration), Earthquake Response Spectra, Damping and Energy Losses
Modeling of Soil during Cyclic Loading (LVM, LHM, Elastoplastic Models)
Modeling of Soil during Cyclic Loading (Bilinear, Hyperbolic, Ramberg-Osgood Models, Masing Criterions); Wave Velocities, Moduli and Damping at Small Strains (Elastic Moduli and Wave Velocities)
Wave Velocities, Moduli and Damping at Small Strains (Gmax in Clays, Effect of Aging, Number of Cycles; Small Strain Field Tests)
Mid-term
Wave Velocities, Moduli and Damping at Small Strains (Small Strain Field Tests)
Wave Velocities, Moduli and Damping at Large Strains, Wave Equation and Wave Velocity
Elastic Reflection and Transmission/Refraction of Traveling Waves (Boundary Problems), Radiation Damping
Kelvin–Voigt Model in Site Response Analysis and Linear Analysis, Wave Energy
Equivalent Linear Analysis, Nonlinear Analysis
Site Response Analysis using Equivalent Linear (EQL) Method with RSseismic / Strata
Input Motion Decision, Design Code Review
Final Exam

courses.title: Advanced Geomechanics
courses.text: The purpose of this course is to introduce students to advanced soil behavior and critical state soil mechanics. Building on fundamental soil mechanics, the course examines stress- and state-dependent responses of sands and clays, including dilative and contractive behavior, drained and undrained strength, and stress paths. Through the framework of critical state soil mechanics and simple constitutive models (e.g., Mohr–Coulomb and Cam-clay), students will learn how to interpret laboratory tests, characterize soil strength and deformation, and develop a mechanistic basis for advanced geotechnical analysis and design.
outline: Course Introduction, Phase Properties and Relationships
Fundamental Engineering Characterization of Soils, Sand-Like Soils
Clay-Like Soils – Minerals, Atterberg Limits
Mixed Soils, Effective Stress – Particle Forces
Effective Stress – Unsaturated Soils, Back to Terzaghi 1D Consolidation
Shear Strength of Soil (Cohesionless Soils, Cohesive Soils)
Elasticity and 2D to 3D Space – Stress and Strain
Mid-term
2D Stress Path – Practical Problems
3D Stress Path – Conventional Laboratory Tests
Critical State – Cohesionless Soils: State Parameters, Taylor's Equation, Dilatancy
Foundations of Plasticity, Critical State – Cohesive Soils (Cam Clay)
Cam Clay (Yield Surface) and Critical State: Volume Change in Clay, Triaxial Tests (Drained vs Undrained)
Undrained Strength of Clay with Cam Clay, Cam Clay Model Parameters
Review
Final Exam

teachingPhilosophy: Even at this very moment, cutting-edge technologies and newly published research continue to expand the existing boundaries of knowledge, imposing upon us the obligations to never stop learning. It is my belief, then, that a true educator should be a fast tracker of all recent developments in their field and become a forerunner in delivering the new knowledge to their students. This requires a careful process in which the most essential information is sorted out of a superabundant supply of new knowledge, necessitating the scholar to have already mastered the fundamental rubrics and theories of the field. It is this belief that bases my teaching goal: I want to resolve the gap between existing and new research and alleviate the inconsistency between fundamental theories and practical industry approach, ultimately aiding my students to become more self-directed engineers capable of resolving novel challenges they will inevitably encounter out in the real world.

culture.lead:
Research begins the moment we confront what "doesn't work."

We do not merely focus on successful outcomes. Instead, we cultivate a culture where unsolved challenges are brought to light, and their root causes are rigorously explored through fundamentals. GEHL fosters an environment of freedom—not as a lack of order or neglect, but as systematic autonomy that supports self-directed growth through teamwork. We provide flexible yet clear guidelines that allow students to fully immerse themselves in their research and evolve independently.

We welcome students who are fueled by a passion for discovery, who ponder deeply and relentlessly, and who seek to transcend their own limits through collaborative dialogue with their colleagues.

lookingFor.title: Teamwork
lookingFor.text: We share data, code, failures, and credit. Progress in a centrifuge lab is a team result.

lookingFor.title: A mechanics-oriented mindset
lookingFor.text: Tools change; equilibrium, compatibility, and constitutive behavior do not. We want people who reason from mechanics first.

lookingFor.title: Logical communication
lookingFor.text: Students who can articulate their thoughts clearly based on "Why" and "How," while remaining flexible enough to embrace the opinions of others.

lookingFor.title: Persistence and resilience
lookingFor.text: Tests fail, models diverge, and reviewers push back. Keep going, and learn from what broke.

lookingFor.title: Clear storytelling
lookingFor.text: Research has to be explained to colleagues, practitioners, and the public.

lookingFor.title: Self-motivation
lookingFor.text: Curiosity and a sense of engineering responsibility carry a project further than any schedule.

culture.positions:
We welcome undergraduate interns, graduate students (M.S. and Ph.D.), and postdoc researchers who are interested in geotechnical earthquake engineering and natural hazards. Character and mindset matter as much as academic record: an inquisitive spirit, persistence, respect, humility, and logical thinking. We are always open to discussing methodologies, research ideas, and emerging topics.

지반지진 및 재해 연구실(GEHL)은 지반지진공학 및 자연재해에 관한 공학적 연구에 관심 있는 학부인턴/대학원생/박사후연구원을 모집합니다. GEHL은 연구자로서 순수한 열정과 지적 호기심, 그리고 공학자로서 책임감을 지닌 학생들을 환영합니다. GEHL은 지진/자연재해에 대한 의미 있는 연구로 다음 세 가지를 추구합니다. 

   1. 과학적/역학적 이해를 바탕으로한 지진/자연재해 문제의 메커니즘 분석

   2. 미래에 발생 가능한 지진/지반공학적 위험 예측 및 해결책 제안

   3. 지진/자연재해에 대한 사회기반시설물 및 도시 시스템의 안정성을 평가할 수 있는 효율적/혁신적 방법론 개발

GEHL은 독창적인 방법론, 새로운 연구 아이디어, 그리고 새롭게 떠오르는 주제에 대한 논의를 환영합니다. 연구실 진학 또는 관련 분야 진로 상담을 희망하는 경우, 고길완 교수(kilwanko at kaist.ac.kr)에게 연락주시기 바랍니다.

news.title: New paper in Soil Dynamics and Earthquake Engineering
news.body: New paper "A Probabilistic Energy-Based Framework for Performance-Based Liquefaction Hazard Assessment: From Triggering to Consequence" published in Soil Dynamics and Earthquake Engineering. This study connects liquefaction triggering assessment with ground settlement estimation within a unified probabilistic framework, helping translate seismic hazard into measurable performance outcomes.

news.title: Joined the Editorial Board of IJPMG
news.body:
I am pleased to share that I have joined the Editorial Board of the International Journal of Physical Modelling in Geotechnics.

IJPMG is an international journal associated with Technical Committee TC104 of the International Society for Soil Mechanics and Geotechnical Engineering (ISSMGE). The journal focuses on research in physical modeling in geotechnical engineering, including centrifuge modeling, 1g modeling, and shaking table testing.

As physical modelling has been an important part of my research, I look forward to contributing to the journal and supporting high-quality research in this field.

teaching.goal: World-best decision makers and leaders in geotechnical engineering
teaching.lead: Courses are built on the experiential learning cycle and use every sense a student has. Each class moves from feeling to talking to thinking to doing: a concrete experience, reflection and discussion on it, a concept that explains it, and an experiment that tests it. The aim is engineers who can make decisions about seismic and natural hazard risk, not only calculate it.

cycle.d: Centrifuge tests, laboratory experiments, and earthquake damage are the starting point. Homework asks students to run an experiment or study a case history before the theory is introduced.
Case histories from past earthquakes are introduced and discussed in class, so that students put what they saw into words and compare interpretations.
Recorded motions, site response, and the mechanics behind them turn the observation into a concept the student can carry to a new problem.
Students test the concept in new experiments, analyses, and designs, which produces the next concrete experience and closes the loop.

teaching.quote: Learning through Experience, Growing through Discussion, and Opening the future through Innovation
